variants.name: Type-set constraints on type parameters (Go 1.18)
variants.idiom_name: interface constraint with type union and ~T approximation
variants.implementation_notes: Go expresses a type's properties as its method set and, since 1.18, as the type set of an interface used as a constraint: interface{ ~int | ~float64 } denotes every type whose underlying type is int or float64, comparable denotes the comparable types, and an operation is available on a type parameter exactly when every type in its type set supports it - so generic code selects behaviour from the properties of T without a base type and without virtual dispatch. Generalized interfaces are constraint-only and cannot be used as variable types. Where each type needs its own code path rather than a shared body, an interface value or a type switch (switch v := x.(type)) is what replaces the descriptor; use the type-set form for algorithms over a family of types.
pitfalls: A type parameter exposes only what its constraint declares: a method that every type in the set happens to have is not callable, so every operation the algorithm needs must be written into the constraint interface (the restriction the Go 1.18 release notes list).
A generalized interface with unions or ~T elements may only be used as a constraint - var n Number does not compile - and a type parameter may not be embedded in a struct or interface.

Since Go 1.20 a type argument that merely supports == (such as any) satisfies comparable, so a comparable-constrained body can panic on a non-comparable dynamic type even though the constraint looked airtight.

variants.name: Structural interfaces plus type switches (pre-generics)
variants.idiom_name: implicit interface satisfaction + type switch / type assertion
variants.implementation_notes: Before generics - and still the right tool when behaviour is per-type rather than shared - a type's property is its method set: an interface value carries the operations, and interface satisfaction is structural, so a type implements an interface merely by having the methods, with no declaration of intent. That is exactly the non-intrusive property of a descriptor, and the stdlib relies on it (io.Writer, sort.Interface, fmt.Stringer, error). Code reads the property back with a type assertion or a type switch (if s, ok := v.(Sizer); ok), and since a trait cannot hold associated types or per-type constants, those become methods or an explicit map keyed by reflect.Type.
pitfalls: Value receivers and pointer receivers give different method sets: a value of a type with pointer methods does not satisfy the interface, and the mismatch surprises callers who pass values.
A type switch falls through to default for a type nobody described, so the compile-time 'unsupported type' error of a descriptor becomes a silent default branch (or a panic on a failed assertion).
An interface holding a typed nil is not equal to nil, so a property check can pass and the very next call panics on a nil receiver.
